name: Inca Trail to Machu Picchu
permit_note: Permits only through a registered operator; licensed guide required; closed every February.
why: Original Inca stone paths through cloud forest and high passes, ending at the Sun Gate above Machu Picchu.
flags: best months from travel sites, not official
ascent from Wikipedia only
days: usually four, sometimes five
stops along the way from Wikipedia; no official route page found

name: Tour du Mont Blanc
permit_note: No permit; book huts early in peak season; carry ID for border crossings.
why: A circuit around the Mont Blanc massif through three countries, linking mountain huts and villages.
flags: official 10,000 m may be total difference, not gain only
days: official site says about 10, Wikipedia 9–14
variants over Fenêtre d'Arpette or Col des Fours reach 2,665 m

name: Torres del Paine W Trek
permit_note: Park ticket bought online ahead, plus a booked refugio or campsite for every night.
why: Named for its W shape through the Ascencio, Francés and Grey valleys, to the Paine towers and Grey Glacier.
flags: no official total distance
high point from trail guides only
rules change within a season
days: Chile's tourism board says 4–6, Wikipedia 3–5

name: Everest Base Camp
permit_note: Sagarmatha National Park fee plus a local Khumbu permit; whether a guide is required is disputed.
why: From Lukla via Namche Bazaar and Tengboche to the south base camp of Mount Everest.
flags: distance from operators only
guide rule disputed
stops along the way from Wikipedia; no official itinerary found

name: Milford Track
permit_note: Huts must be booked for the Great Walks season; no camping; one direction only.
why: A Great Walk through glacier-carved valleys over Omanui/McKinnon Pass, with a side trip to 580 m Sutherland Falls.
flags: 53.5 km is the sum of DOC stages
1,154 m is the pass shelter; the pass itself is about 1,140 m

name: Tongariro Alpine Crossing
permit_note: No permit; free booking recommended and required for shuttles.
why: A day hike across active volcanic terrain on Mount Tongariro, in a World Heritage national park.
flags: best months inferred from DOC winter warnings

name: Kumano Kodo (Nakahechi)
permit_note: No permit; book lodgings ahead, walk-ins are rare.
why: A pilgrimage route to Kumano Hongu Taisha, recorded since the early 10th century; UNESCO World Heritage since 2004.
flags: no official figure for the highest point

name: Laugavegur Trail
permit_note: No permit; confirmed hut or campsite booking expected; open roughly late June to mid-September.
why: Often called Iceland's most popular hiking trail, crossing the southern highlands from the coloured mountains of Landmannalaugar to Þórsmörk.
flags: difficulty is a judgement; no official grade
no official count of hikers

name: West Highland Way
permit_note: No permit; camping in parts of Loch Lomond needs a permit from March to September.
why: Scotland's first officially designated long-distance route, opened in 1980.
flags: best months from a guidebook

name: Camino de Santiago (Camino Francés)
permit_note: No permit; a pilgrim credential opens pilgrim hostels and earns the Compostela.
why: The most popular route of the Way of St. James pilgrimage; UNESCO World Heritage since 1993.
flags: no official total distance

name: Tiger Leaping Gorge High Trail
permit_note: No permit for the High Trail; Middle Tiger Leaping Gorge closed since April 2025.
why: One of the world's deepest river canyons, cut by the upper Yangtze between Jade Dragon and Haba Snow Mountains.
flags: longer published distances include the Middle Gorge descent, closed since April 2025
current access to the end point unconfirmed
stops along the way from travel guides only; no official source found

name: Half Dome
permit_note: Lottery permit required when the cables are up (late May to mid-October).
why: A granite dome rising nearly 5,000 feet above Yosemite Valley; the last 400 feet climb steel cables.
